activator.label: Activator & Alerts
activator.description: Original practice questions authored for the Hansa corpus integration from Microsoft Fabric Activator and Real-Time Hub documentation harvested by the deep-research corpus. Covers what Activator is, where its data comes from (streams, dashboards, semantic models, querysets), how rules and triggers work, the actions it can take, and its lifecycle surfaces (Git, capacity, monitoring). No video anchors.

questions.title: What Activator is for
questions.prompt: Which statement describes Fabric Activator?

options.text: A surface that watches data as it changes and automatically takes actions — like alerts — when conditions are met.
options.why: Correct. Activator's definition is data-change detection plus automatic action.

options.text: A batch ETL engine for warehouse tables.
options.why: That is pipeline/dataflow territory.

options.text: A semantic-model visualization type.
options.why: Activator is not a visual.

options.text: A source-control service.
options.why: Git is; Activator only integrates with it.

questions.explanation: Activator = monitor + condition + automatic action, on streaming or periodically updated data.

questions.title: Four ways in
questions.prompt: Which of these are documented ways to get data into Activator? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: An eventstream, via the Activator destination or Real-Time hub alerts.
options.why: Correct — streaming data is Activator's primary path.

options.text: A real-time dashboard tile.

options.text: A Power BI semantic model's data.

options.why: Incorrect — file watching is not a documented Activator data source.

questions.explanation: The documented sources: eventstreams, real-time dashboard tiles, semantic-model data, and KQL querysets — not file watching.

questions.title: Alerting the model, not the stream
questions.prompt: Finance wants an alert when a Power BI report's KPI (from an imported semantic model, refreshed daily) crosses a threshold. Which Activator path serves that?

options.text: Getting data from the Power BI semantic model into Activator and defining the alert on it — evaluated when the model data changes.
options.why: Correct. The documented semantic-model path covers exactly this batch-refresh alerting.

options.text: An eventstream reading the model.
options.why: Eventstreams ingest streaming sources; they do not read semantic models.

options.text: A materialized view over the model.
options.why: Materialized views live in Eventhouses over KQL tables.

options.text: A Real-Time dashboard bound to the model.
options.why: Real-time dashboards bind to streaming/KQL data, not imported models.

questions.explanation: Not everything alert-worthy streams: the semantic-model path lets Activator evaluate imported-model data on its refresh cadence.

options.text: Query → pivot → render.

options.why: Correct. Data-condition alerting is Activator's job; run-outcome alerting belongs to pipelines.

options.text: Nothing — they are the same feature.
options.why: The watched objects differ fundamentally: data versus runs.

options.text: Activator replaces pipeline monitoring entirely.
options.why: Run-level monitoring remains its own surface.

options.text: Activator only alerts on pipeline failures.
options.why: That is the narrower pipeline-alerts job.

options.text: Create one Activator item per substation manually.
options.why: That scales badly; grouping is built into the rule model.

options.text: Substation grouping is not supported; only global alerts exist.

options.text: Grouping happens in the dashboard visual instead.
options.why: Visual grouping is presentation, not rule evaluation.

questions.title: Noise discipline
questions.prompt: Raw voltage spikes are benign; the duty analyst should be alerted on the five-minute average crossing a threshold. Where should that aggregation live so the alert stays meaningful?

options.text: Upstream of the alert — in the eventstream aggregate or a maintained view — so the alert evaluates a stabilized series.
options.why: Correct. Alert quality follows signal quality; the windowed aggregate belongs in the pipeline or store, not the alert condition.

options.text: Inside the alert condition as a custom average over raw events.
options.why: The condition evaluates provided values; windowing is not its job.

options.text: Nowhere — alert on every raw spike.
options.why: That is the noise problem the requirement rules out.

options.text: In the email subject line text.
options.why: Presentation cannot fix an unstable signal.

questions.explanation: The windowed aggregate is pipeline/storage work; the alert then evaluates a stable signal per its trigger.

questions.title: The missing-event alert
questions.prompt: Operations needs an alert when a substation stops reporting for more than 15 minutes — an absence of data, not a value condition. Which design is defensible with the documented pieces?

options.text: Compute last-seen per substation in the data layer (a KQL queryset summarizing max(Timestamp) per substation, filtered to those older than 15 minutes) and alert on that queryset results.
options.why: Correct. Absence must be made into a signal: the data layer exposes who has gone quiet as rows, and queryset alerts evaluate them.

options.text: An Activator condition that evaluates no-events-arrived on the stream directly.
options.why: Conditions evaluate provided values; the platform does not natively express absence on a stream — expose it as data first.

options.text: A Filter node that drops the quiet substations so their absence is noticed.
options.why: Dropping events hides the signal; it cannot create an absence alert.

options.text: A daily manual review of the dashboard.
options.why: Manual review is not an alert and loses the 15-minute requirement.

questions.explanation: Absence-of-data is not a value condition: compute the last-seen signal in the data layer (KQL), then let Activator alert on the queryset that surfaces the quiet substations.

options.text: Power BI has no alerting at all.

options.text: Report alerts are always lower latency than Activator.

questions.title: The false-positive problem
questions.prompt: After go-live, the on-call channel is flooded by transient spikes. Which corrective design is soundest?

options.text: Alert on a stabilized signal (aggregated upstream) and/or add condition hysteresis (e.g., sustained threshold rather than single-event), then re-test against the run history.
options.why: Correct. Signal stabilization plus sustained-condition logic are the standard noise fixes, verifiable in run history.

options.text: Remove the alert entirely.
options.why: That removes coverage, not noise.

options.text: Add more recipients to share the pain.
options.why: Recipients do not change signal quality.

options.text: Shorten the evaluation interval to catch more spikes.
options.why: That increases noise, not signal.

questions.explanation: Noise is fixed upstream (stabilize the signal) and in the condition (sustained evaluation), then verified in history.

questions.title: Percent change conditions
questions.prompt: An alert should fire when a metric rises more than 10% compared to its previous value. Which condition design fits?

options.text: A condition comparing the current value against the prior value — the data source must expose both (e.g., via the query or stream payload), because the condition evaluates provided values.
options.why: Correct. The condition compares values it is given; computing the delta belongs to the data path if the platform does not provide it directly.

options.text: Assume Activator stores history and computes percentages automatically.
options.why: Do not assume history semantics; design the data to carry what the condition needs.

options.text: Create two alerts and compare their emails.
options.why: Emails are actions, not a comparison engine.

options.text: Ask the dashboard theme to color the change.
options.why: Presentation, again, is not evaluation.

questions.explanation: Conditions evaluate what the data provides — percent-change designs must surface both values (or the delta) in the monitored data.
